name: Plastic footprint
seoTitle: Plastic footprint Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Plastic footprint: work out refill packets from the PET bottles and the plastic bags. A free ecology calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Plastic footprint calculator the PET bottles, the plastic bags, the food wrappers and the yogurt containers and it returns refill packets. It is built for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Plastic footprint calculator work?
sections.html:
The Plastic footprint calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports refill packets in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the PET bottles, the plastic bags, the food wrappers and the yogurt containers.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Plastic footprint calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Refill packets=-36 ÷ 17 × PET bottles − 8 ÷ 17 × plastic bags − 80 ÷ 17 × shampoo ÷ shower gel ÷ cosmetics bottles − 1 ÷ 17 × cotton swabs − 4 ÷ 17 × disposable cutlery − 120 ÷ 17 × detergent, cleaning products bottles − 15 ÷ 17 × food wrappers − 4 ÷ 24837 × toys, furnitures etc. − 24 ÷ 17 × plastic plates − 1 ÷ 34 × straws + (4 ÷ 24837) × total − 32 ÷ 17 × take-away plastic box − 20 ÷ 17 × take-away plastic cup − 20 ÷ 17 × toothbrushes − 15 ÷ 17 × toothpastes − 15 ÷ 17 × yogurt containers
Which is=75 × total

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose PET bottles = 0 wks, Plastic bags = 0 wks, Food wrappers = 0 wks and Yogurt containers = 0 wks. Working through the relationship above gives Which is = 750 kg.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Which is = 750 kg should be roughly the size you expected from PET bottles = 0 wks and Plastic bags = 0 wks.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Plastic footprint calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the PET bottles, the plastic bags and the food wrappers — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Plastic footprint calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns refill packets, derived from the PET bottles, the plastic bags and the food wrappers. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Plastic footprint calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the PET bottles, the plastic bags, the food wrappers and the yogurt containers, which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter PET bottles in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. PET bottles opens in weeks and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Which is = 750 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Plastic footprint calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
